title: Lexical Scope
description: Where scope is decided, shadowing and closures

options: At runtime, each time a function is called
At author time, by where functions and blocks are written in the code
When the function is first assigned to a variable
When the garbage collector runs
questions.explanation: Lexical scope is defined at lexing/author time: the nesting of functions and blocks in your source code decides which variables each piece of code can see. Where or how a function is later called does not change it (with the exception of cheats like eval and with).

questions.explanation: inner was written inside outer, so its scope chain is inner → outer → global, regardless of where fn() is called. The look-up for x stops at the first match, outer's x.

questions.prompt: What is it called when an inner scope declares a variable with the same name as one in an outer scope?
options: Hoisting
Shadowing
Currying
Bubbling
questions.explanation: The inner variable shadows the outer one: scope look-up stops at the first match, so inside the inner scope the outer variable with that name is unreachable by its plain name.

questions.explanation: show was declared at the top level, so its scope chain is show → global. The value inside run is not visible to it, because JavaScript uses lexical (not dynamic) scope. The RHS look-up fails and throws a ReferenceError.

questions.explanation: var is function-scoped (here: global), so there is only one i, shared by all three callbacks. By the time the timers fire the loop has finished and i is 3. Declaring the loop variable with let creates a fresh binding per iteration and logs 0 1 2 — prefer let/const in modern code.

questions.prompt: Which statement about let and const is true?
options: They are function-scoped like var
They are block-scoped and cannot be accessed before their declaration (temporal dead zone)
They are not hoisted at all and are always undefined before declaration
They automatically create properties on the global object
questions.explanation: let and const are block-scoped. Their declarations are hoisted, but the binding stays uninitialized until the declaration runs; accessing it earlier (the temporal dead zone) throws a ReferenceError. Unlike top-level var, they do not create properties on window/globalThis.

options: A function that has finished executing
A function together with access to the variables of the scope it was defined in, even after that scope has returned
A way to make object properties private using Symbol
A block of code wrapped in curly braces
questions.explanation: A closure is a function that keeps access to its lexical scope even when executed outside of it. That is why a returned inner function can still read and update variables of the outer function that already returned.
Each call to counter() creates a new scope with its own count. a has been called three times (the third call is inside console.log) so it returns 3, while b's separate count returns 1.

questions.prompt: Why is using eval() or with considered bad for scope?
options: They are not supported in modern browsers
They modify lexical scope at runtime, which defeats engine optimizations and makes code hard to reason about
They only work in strict mode
They make all variables global constants
questions.explanation: eval can inject declarations into the current scope and with creates a scope from an object at runtime. Because the engine can no longer know scopes ahead of time, it must skip many optimizations. with is forbidden in strict mode, and strict-mode eval gets its own scope.
